entities.label: Idea
entities.summary:
Hedonism, a philosophical and ethical worldview asserting that pleasure is the highest good and the proper aim of human life, emerged prominently in Ancient Greece, particularly through the teachings of Aristippus of Cyrene (c. 435–356 BCE) and later Epicurus (341–270 BCE). Far from a monolithic doctrine, it encompasses diverse interpretations, from the radical pursuit of immediate bodily gratification by the Cyrenaics to the Epicurean emphasis on tranquil, lasting pleasure achieved through moderation and the absence of pain (ataraxia). This fundamental inquiry into the nature of happiness and the good life has resonated across millennia, challenging prevailing moral and religious frameworks and shaping Western thought on ethics and human motivation.

The initial formulation by Aristippus of Cyrene, a student of Socrates, posited that present, physical pleasure was the only intrinsically good thing, advocating for a life focused on intense, immediate sensations. His school, the Cyrenaics, flourished in the 4th century BCE, developing a nuanced taxonomy of pleasures and pains. Later, Epicurus founded his school, The Garden, in Athens around 307 BCE, directly engaging with and refining hedonistic principles. Epicurus argued for a more refined hedonism, where the highest pleasure was a state of serenity and freedom from fear and suffering, achieved through philosophical contemplation, friendship, and the avoidance of excess, rather than the pursuit of fleeting sensory delights. This distinction was crucial, moving the discourse from crude indulgence to a more sophisticated understanding of well-being.
